slides.title: Comparison chart, as one reusable function
slides.code:
def make_comparison_chart(df, group_col, value_col, out_path):
    """Bar chart of group means; returns the summary table."""
    summary = df.groupby(group_col).agg(
        mean_value=(value_col, "mean"),
        n=("room_id", "count"),
    ).round(2)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
    ax.bar(summary.index.astype(str), summary["mean_value"], color="#3D8DFF")
    # ... axis labels, a title, and fig.savefig(out_path) as usual
    plt.close(fig)
    return summary
slides.explainHead: group_col and value_col are parameters, not fixed names
slides.explainBody: This exact function is called again in the self-check with "floor" instead of "zone", and again in Studio time with your own dataset's column names -- only the arguments change, never the body.
slides.teaching: Point at the docstring and both type-hint-free-but-documented parameters -- remind students the Week 4 convention (docstring + basic type hint on every function) still applies.

slides.title: Anatomy of a groupby(...).agg(...) call

parts.label: Result row
parts.body: One row per group -- returned so the caller can reuse it.

parts.label: Source table
parts.body: The full room-level DataFrame, passed in as a parameter.

parts.label: Groups rows by column
parts.body: group_col is a parameter -- "zone" today, "floor" in the self-check.

parts.label: Named aggregation
parts.body: Expands to the two named aggregations from the previous slide.

slides.teaching: Walk the four chips left to right: the result table, the source table, the grouping parameter, and the named aggregations -- this is the exact call inside make_comparison_chart.

slides.title: Predict: what does the n column look like after .round(2)?
slides.question: After .round(2) runs on the table, what dtype is column n?
options: float64 -- .round(2) rounds every column in the table
int64 -- .round(2) only rounds floating-point columns, n stays whole
Raises a TypeError -- round() cannot run on a table with mixed dtypes
n is dropped -- round() keeps only the column it can round
slides.why: Verified: n is already int64 from .count(); .round(2) only touches float64 columns, so n still prints as 12, not 12.00.
slides.teaching: Most students assume round() either touches every column or errors on a mixed-dtype table -- neither happens; it silently skips columns that are not floats.

slides.title: plt.close(fig), defined
slides.definition: Releases one saved figure from memory. It does not delete the saved file -- fig.savefig() already wrote that to disk -- it only frees the fig object itself.

example.head: Why it matters here
example.body: make_comparison_chart runs three times today: once for zone, once for floor in the self-check, once for your own dataset. Without plt.close(fig) inside the function, all three figures would stay open in memory instead of being released after each save.

slides.note: A script that plots once and exits would never notice a missing plt.close(fig) -- it only matters once a plotting function is called repeatedly, exactly as it is here.
slides.teaching: Point out this line was easy to skim past inside the function on the previous slides -- it earns its own slide because it only matters once a plotting function runs more than once, which is exactly what today's studio does three times.

slides.title: Relationship: color the scatter by zone
slides.code:
def make_relationship_chart(df, x_col, y_col, group_col, out_path):
    """Scatter x_col vs y_col, colored by group_col."""
    plot_df = df.dropna(subset=[y_col])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
    for group_value, color in zip(["North", "South"], ["#3D8DFF", "#C9473A"]):
        subset = plot_df[plot_df[group_col] == group_value]
        ax.scatter(subset[x_col], subset[y_col], color=color,
                   label=f"{group_value} (n={len(subset)})")
    # ... annotate two outliers, label axes, and save (next slide)
slides.explainHead: One loop replaces two separate ax.scatter calls
slides.explainBody: zip(...) pairs each group name with its color, so the loop runs once per zone instead of writing ax.scatter twice by hand. subset filters to just that zone's rows first -- the same boolean-filter pattern from Week 4.
slides.teaching: Ask why south is n=11, not 12, here -- room R206's missing energy value is dropped by the dropna(subset=[y_col]) line, the same missing value from Week 4's trustworthiness interview.

slides.title: Relationship: annotate R306, then save
slides.code:
r306 = df.loc[df["room_id"] == "R306"].iloc[0]
    ax.annotate(f"R306: {r306[x_col]} m2, {r306[y_col]} kWh/m2/yr",
                xy=(r306[x_col], r306[y_col]), xytext=(52, 400),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
    # ... a second ax.annotate call labels R309 (Studio 3)

    ax.set_xlabel("Room area (m2)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Energy use intensity (kWh/m2/yr)")
    ax.legend(loc="lower right")
    fig.savefig(out_path)
    plt.close(fig)
slides.explainHead: xy is the point pointed AT; xytext is the label's own spot
slides.explainBody: df.loc[...].iloc[0] pulls R306's single row, then r306[x_col] and r306[y_col] read its actual area and energy values into the arrow's target. The next slide explodes this exact call; Studio 3 asks you to write a second one for R309 yourselves.
slides.teaching: Remind students R309 is North zone (120.0 m2, 68.0 kWh/m2/yr) -- a student who mislabels its zone will place it in the wrong-colored group when they check their own scatter.

slides.title: Anatomy of an ax.annotate(...) call

parts.label: The axes being annotated
parts.body: Same ax as scatter() or bar() -- one more method call on it.

parts.label: Draws a label plus an arrow
parts.body: One call adds both the text and the connecting arrow.

parts.label: The text string
parts.body: Often an f-string built from one room's own values, like R306's.

parts.label: Point pointed AT
parts.body: Where the arrow's tip touches -- e.g. (r306[x_col], r306[y_col]).

parts.label: Where the text itself sits
parts.body: Where the label box sits -- swapping this with xy is the top mistake.

slides.teaching: Walk chip by chip: ax is the same object as the scatter above; annotate() bundles the label and arrow; xy is the aiming point, xytext is where the box of text sits -- swapping the two doesn't error, it just points at the wrong place.

slides.title: update(frame): everything ax.clear() erases
slides.code:
def update(frame):
    ax.clear()
    shown = plot_df.iloc[: frame + 1]
    ax.bar(shown["room_id"], shown[value_col], color="#3D8DFF")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.5, n_rooms - 0.5)
    ax.set_ylim(0, plot_df[value_col].max() * 1.05)
    ax.set_xlabel("Room (sorted low to high)")
    ax.set_ylabel(f"{value_col} (kWh/m2/yr)")
    ax.set_title(f"Rooms reporting in: {frame + 1} of {n_rooms}")
slides.explainHead: ax.clear() erases the title and limits too, not just the bars
slides.explainBody: Every line here after ax.clear() has to be rewritten every single frame -- labels, limits, and title included. Skip one and it silently vanishes for all but the first frame; this is Studio 4's single most common slip.
slides.teaching: Ask what the .gif would look like if ax.set_xlim/ax.set_ylim were left out of update() -- the axes would rescale to fit each frame's own smaller data, making bar heights look inconsistent even though the values are not changing.

slides.title: One function wraps setup, update, and save
slides.code:
def build_progressive_animation(df, value_col, out_path):
    """Animate rooms sorted by value; save as .gif."""
    plot_df = df.dropna(subset=[value_col])
    plot_df = plot_df.sort_values(value_col)
    plot_df = plot_df.reset_index(drop=True)
    n_rooms = len(plot_df)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    def update(frame):
        ...  # clears and redraws ax -- previous slide
    ani = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=n_rooms, interval=200)
    ani.save(out_path, writer="pillow", fps=5)
    plt.close(fig)
    return n_rooms
slides.explainHead: fig, ax, n_rooms, and plot_df are all built ONCE
slides.explainBody: Only the lines inside update() rerun every frame. FuncAnimation calls update once per frame, then ani.save(..., writer="pillow") writes every frame into one .gif -- no live window required.
slides.teaching: Point out fig, ax, n_rooms, and plot_df sit outside update() -- created once, then reused every frame; only update()'s own lines repeat.

slides.title: Call it once, and write your caption

CAPTION = ("Radley Hall's 23 measured rooms, revealed one at a time from lowest "
           "to highest energy use intensity; the final bar is room R306, "
           "the server-closet outlier.")
n_frames = build_progressive_animation(df, "energy_kwh_m2_yr", "energy_reporting_animation.gif")

23
Radley Hall's 23 measured rooms, revealed one at a time from lowest to highest energy use intensity; the final bar is room R306, the server-closet outlier.
slides.explainHead: A caption is text, because a report cannot embed motion
slides.explainBody: n_frames confirms the animation ran through all 23 measured rooms and that the .gif was written to disk. CAPTION is what actually goes into your written report -- a report is text, so the .gif needs a one-sentence description standing in for what a reader would see if they opened the file.
slides.teaching: Require the printed CAPTION line as evidence the animation was actually run and inspected, not merely saved and forgotten.

slides.title: "Captioned," defined for this week

left.head: Two required parts
left.body: (1) an in-figure title on the animation itself (e.g., "Rooms reporting in: N of 23"), visible while the .gif plays; and (2) one printed CAPTION string, 1-2 sentences, describing what changes frame to frame and naming any outlier that appears.

right.head: Why both are required
right.body: The in-figure title orients someone watching the .gif directly. The printed caption is what goes into your written report, since a report is text and cannot embed a playing animation.

slides.teaching: Point out this is exactly why cell [5] both sets ax.set_title() inside update() AND prints a separate CAPTION string -- two different audiences, two different places.

slides.title: Predict: what happens when np.histogram meets a NaN?
slides.code:
counts, edges = np.histogram(
    df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"], bins=6
)
print(counts)
slides.question: This column still has one missing value. What happens?
options: Prints [13 9 0 0 0 1], same as Studio 1 -- np.histogram skips NaN automatically
Raises a ValueError -- np.histogram can't auto-detect a range that includes NaN
Prints six zeros -- one NaN forces every bin count to 0
Silently drops the NaN row and renumbers the bins -- 23 rooms instead of 24
slides.why: Verified: np.histogram (unlike ax.hist()) does not filter non-finite values -- it raises: autodetected range of [nan, nan] is not finite.
slides.teaching: Most students assume np.histogram behaves like ax.hist() and quietly skips the NaN -- it does not. Let them commit to an answer before revealing the real crash on the next slide.

slides.title: An AI 'shortcut' that crashes
slides.output: ValueError: autodetected range of [nan, nan] is not finite
slides.explainHead: No .dropna() -- and np.histogram refuses to guess
slides.explainBody: This is the exact column from Studio 1, without .dropna(). np.histogram tries to auto-detect the data's min and max first; with one NaN present, that auto-detected range is itself NaN, so it raises immediately rather than guessing a range.
slides.teaching: Let a student run this live and read the traceback out loud before explaining it -- reading the actual error, not guessing, is the habit this cell is building.

slides.title: AI-code audit: diagnose and repair
slides.prompt: Complete cell [7] of your handout: repair the crash above and explain the gap it reveals.
steps: Read the ValueError message word by word -- what does "autodetected range" refer to?
Explain why ax.hist() in Studio 1 did not raise this same error on the identical column.
Apply the one-line fix (add .dropna()) and confirm the counts match [13 9 0 0 0 1].
Record this defect in your AI-use record as one you would reject from an AI suggestion, and why.
slides.teaching: The answer to step 2: Axes.hist() filters non-finite values internally before it ever calls np.histogram; a bare np.histogram() call does not. The two are not interchangeable on data with missing values, even though they look equivalent.

slides.title: Accessibility check: meaning survives without color

left.head: REDUNDANT ENCODING
left.body: Use position, shape, line style, direct labels, or annotation in addition to color. A grayscale printout should preserve the comparison.

right.head: ACCESSIBLE EXPORT
right.body: Use descriptive titles, axes + units, sufficient contrast, and alt text that states the chart's purpose and main pattern—not every pixel.

slides.teaching: Show one figure in grayscale or ask students to squint: if the categories disappear, color is carrying too much meaning.
